title: Practice traditions, closed
hook: chant, bow, retreat, pilgrimage, perfections, vows

segments.voice: Yesterday, plan your retreat: a set time, a protected place, one practice, and a way back.

Lay these past weeks out on a table like objects from a long trip. A chant sheet in Pali. A page of the Heart Sutra, marked for a wooden drum. The mani, sung. The name of Amitabha, walked around a hall. A bow, from a small nod to the full length of the floor. A long retreat in noble silence, and a sesshin with sore legs and tea at the end. A map of pilgrim roads: Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar, the island of temples, the mountain. The perfections, one a day. Moon days. Vows for others. A funeral chant, a memorial altar, a meal chant, and yesterday's plan. That's a lot to carry home. Today's step is small and honest: pick up one thing from the table.
screen: `CHANT, BOW, RETREAT.` → `PILGRIMAGE, PERFECTIONS, VOWS.` → `PICK UP ONE THING.`

segments.voice: The tradition has a word for all of this: bhavana. It's often translated meditation, but it's wider than sitting. It means cultivation, bringing something into being, the way a gardener brings up a plant. Chanting is bhavana. So is bowing, giving, keeping a precept on a moon day. Every practice here is a different kind of gardening. Why one and not all? The Dhammapada has a picture for how good grows, in Max Müller's words: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled." The verse is about not thinking little of small good acts. A drop doesn't fill a pot. A drop, again and again, does. A month of tasting is a sampler. One practice, kept, fills the pot. How to choose? Some teachers put it simply: start with what you'll actually do. Not the most impressive practice; the one that fits your mornings, your body, your house. A short chant you can say while the kettle boils may grow further than a ten-day retreat you never book. And the schools don't ask you to pick a team. These weeks, a Theravada chant sat next to a Zen drum and a Pure Land name, each taught on its own terms. Choosing one to deepen isn't a verdict on the others. It's just where your water-drops land for now. And from tomorrow, the festival year comes round again, starting with the full moon of Vesak.
screen: `BHAVANA: BRINGING INTO BEING.` · `A DROP, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `START WITH WHAT YOU'LL DO.` · then, large: `CHOOSE ONE.`

segments.voice: Let the practices pass slowly through your mind: the chant, the bow, the retreat, the pilgrim road, the perfections, the vows. Don't decide with your head; notice which one your attention leans toward, the way a plant leans toward a window, and when one stays, picture doing it tomorrow for a few minutes, in your real kitchen or your real chair. If more than one comes, keep the first.
Practice traditions. Ways Buddhists of different schools cultivate the path: chanting, bowing, retreat, pilgrimage, the perfections and vows. Today's word.
Your line: choose one. The others will wait for you, too. On to the festivals.

howItsDone: Buddhists in different schools keep practices such as chanting, bowing, meditation retreats, pilgrimage, the perfections and vows, and some settle on one or two that they keep daily, often with a teacher's guidance.

chat.says: You've tried so many Buddhist practices. Shouldn't you do all of them every day?
options: One practice, kept, fills the pot like water-drops; start with the one you'll actually do.
Yes. Each school's practice only works if you do the other schools' practices too.
No. Practices only count on retreat, so save them all up for a long one.
chat.meaning: The Dhammapada's water-drops fill the pot: one practice, kept, grows more than many tasted. Choosing one isn't a verdict on the others.

sesshin.meaning: a Zen week of silent meditation
